paras: The threatened lynching of two brakemen at Mapleton, Dakota, was a confrontation on August 28, 1888, in which a large crowd at the Mapleton depot and the town's city marshal demanded two railroad brakemen accused of causing a tramp's death. The sheriff and district attorney escorting the men refused to give them up, and an inquest jury found that the railroad company was not at fault. The St. Paul Daily Globe reported it under the headline "Ripe for a Lynching."

On August 27 a tramp named Benjamin (printed once as "Bejamin") died after leaving a train between Haggart and Canfield, and two brakemen were accused of ejecting him. Sheriff Barnes and District Attorney Pollock took the brakemen by train to Mapleton for the inquest the next day.

The officers had the train stopped a short distance from Mapleton and went ahead of their prisoners into the town. City Marshal Burdick of Mapleton "rushed excitedly" up to them and demanded the brakemen, saying, "I want them and demand their release to me immediately." The officers refused and told the "large and excited crowd" at the depot that they had come to learn the facts and that the men, if found guilty, would be dealt with "according to law." Judging the crowd satisfied, they brought the brakemen in and opened the inquest.

Testimony at the inquest held that the brakeman had warned two men to keep off the train at Haggart and, while walking toward them near Canfield, saw one "suddenly disappear between the cars." The dead man's partner confirmed this account, and the jury found that the deceased died "through no fault of the railroad company." No report of further action against the brakemen or against anyone in the crowd was found.

The only account found is a special dispatch from Fargo printed on the front page of the St. Paul Daily Globe on August 29. Its deck said that "Mapletonians Came Close to Meeting Out Summary Justice to Two Brakemen," and its opening line credited the "coolness of the officers" with averting a lynching. The dispatch accepted the inquest's finding and blamed the town's "excited pitch" on a "highly colored story" said to have come from the dead man's partner. It gave no race for the brakemen, the tramp or the crowd.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of two brakemen at Mapleton, Dakota
bases: A large, excited crowd gathered at the Mapleton depot and the city marshal demanded two brakemen held for an inquest, which the Globe headlined as a near lynching that officers 'averted' (A2).

No one was killed: the officers refused to surrender the brakemen and the inquest went ahead (A2). The episode is a threatened lynching by a crowd acting on an accusation that the brakemen caused a tramp's death (A2).
Only one report, a special dispatch from Fargo to the St. Paul Daily Globe, describes the episode (A2).

accounts.label: Fargo special dispatch
accounts.gist: A lynching of the brakemen was averted only by the officers' coolness; the inquest found the tramp died through no fault of the railroad, and the town's excitement came from the partner's 'highly colored story'.

accounts.label: Inquest testimony
accounts.gist: The brakeman warned two men off at Haggart and, approaching them near Canfield, saw one suddenly disappear between the cars; the partner substantiated this.

framing.detail: The Globe's headline 'Ripe for a Lynching' treats the crowd as near-lynchers and praises the officers' 'coolness', while presenting the brakemen's version, as confirmed by the inquest, as fact.

record_check.dossier: threatened: a crowd gathered and the marshal demanded the prisoners, but no attack or seizure is reported
The crowd confrontation was Aug. 28, 1888; Aug. 27 was the date of the tramp's death on the train
Crowd gathered at the depot and a demand for the prisoners; no siege or armed assault is described
Two unnamed brakemen (threatened, unharmed); no race given
A large crowd of Mapleton people, with City Marshal Burdick demanding the prisoners
Dakota Territory ('Fargo, Dak.'); ND as present-day equivalent

info: The tramp was ejected or fell from the train on Aug. 27, 1888 ('yesterday' in an Aug. 28 dispatch); the crowd confronted the officers at Mapleton on Aug. 28 ('to-day').
The depot at Mapleton, Dakota; the train had been stopped a short distance from the town. The death occurred on the train between Haggart and Canfield.
Two unnamed brakemen were threatened; none was harmed. The dead tramp is named 'Bejamin'/'Benjamin'. No race is given for anyone.
The brakemen were accused of ejecting a tramp from a train and so causing his death.
A 'large and excited crowd' of Mapleton people at the depot; City Marshal Burdick of Mapleton demanded the brakemen be released to him.
The officers persuaded the crowd that the men would be dealt with by law; the inquest cleared the railroad company. No further action against the brakemen was reported.

sources.note: 'Ripe for a Lynching': special from Fargo, Aug. 28; crowd at Mapleton depot, marshal demands two brakemen, officers refuse, inquest clears railroad.
